title: Integers
subject: Mathematics
summary: Integers are the whole numbers together with their negatives: …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …
points: On a number line, numbers increase to the right and decrease to the left.
Adding a negative moves left; subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive.
The product of two integers with the same sign is positive; with opposite signs it is negative.
mistakes: Thinking −8 is greater than −3 because 8 is greater than 3.
Forgetting that (−2) × (−2) = 4, not −4.

title: Rational numbers
subject: Mathematics
summary: A rational number can be written as p/q where p and q are integers and q is not zero.
points: Every integer and every terminating decimal is rational.
Equivalent forms come from multiplying or dividing the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number.
Between any two rational numbers there is another rational number.
example: 3/4 = 6/8 = 0.75, and −2 = −2/1, so both are rational.
mistakes: Assuming decimals like 0.333… are irrational; 1/3 is rational.

title: HCF and LCM
subject: Mathematics
summary: The highest common factor (HCF) is the largest number dividing two or more numbers exactly; the lowest common multiple (LCM) is the smallest number they all divide.
points: Prime factorisation: HCF takes the lowest power of each common prime, LCM the highest power of every prime.
For two numbers, HCF × LCM = product of the numbers.
HCF is used for splitting into equal groups; LCM for events repeating together.

formulas.name: Relation for two numbers
formulas.expr: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b

example: 12 = 2² × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3², so HCF = 2 × 3 = 6 and LCM = 2² × 3² = 36.
mistakes: Using the highest power for the HCF as well as the LCM.

title: Exponents and powers
subject: Mathematics
summary: An exponent says how many times a number is multiplied by itself: aⁿ means a used as a factor n times.
points: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ and aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ.
(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ and a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero a.
A negative exponent means a reciprocal: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
mistakes: Adding the exponents when multiplying powers of different bases, such as 2³ × 3².

title: Ratio and proportion
subject: Mathematics
summary: A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind; a proportion says two ratios are equal.
points: A ratio 3:5 can be written as the fraction 3/5.
In a proportion a:b = c:d, the product of the extremes equals the product of the means: ad = bc.
The unitary method finds the value of one unit first, then multiplies.

formulas.name: Proportion
formulas.expr: a : b = c : d ⇒ ad = bc

example: If 4 pens cost ₹60, one pen costs ₹15, so 7 pens cost ₹105.
mistakes: Comparing quantities with different units without converting them first.

title: Percentage, profit and loss
subject: Mathematics
summary: Profit or loss compares the selling price with the cost price, usually as a percentage of the cost price.
points: Profit = SP − CP when SP is greater; loss = CP − SP otherwise.
Profit % = (profit ÷ CP) × 100 and loss % = (loss ÷ CP) × 100.
Discount is a reduction on the marked price, not on the cost price.

formulas.name: Profit percentage
formulas.symbols: SP = selling price, CP = cost price

mistakes: Calculating profit percentage on the selling price instead of the cost price.

title: Simple interest
subject: Mathematics
summary: Simple interest is charged only on the original principal, not on interest already earned.
points: Interest = principal × rate × time ÷ 100, with time in years.
Amount = principal + interest.
Compound interest grows faster because interest is added to the principal each period.

formulas.name: Simple interest
formulas.symbols: P = principal, R = rate % per year, T = years

mistakes: Using months as years without dividing by 12.

title: Speed, distance and time
subject: Mathematics
summary: Speed is the distance covered in unit time, so distance = speed × time and time = distance ÷ speed.
points: Units must match: km/h with hours, or m/s with seconds.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, not the average of the speeds.
example: A train covers 180 km in 3 hours, so its speed is 60 km/h.
mistakes: Averaging two speeds directly when the distances are equal.

title: Algebraic expressions
subject: Mathematics
summary: An algebraic expression combines variables, constants and operations, such as 3x + 5.
points: Terms with the same variable and power are like terms and can be combined.
The coefficient is the number multiplying a variable.
Substituting a value means replacing the variable with that number and simplifying.
example: 5x + 3 − 2x = 3x + 3, and if x = 4 the value is 15.
mistakes: Combining unlike terms such as 3x and 3.

title: Linear equations in one variable
subject: Mathematics
summary: A linear equation contains a variable to the first power, and solving it means finding the value that makes both sides equal.
points: Do the same operation to both sides to keep the equation balanced.
Move variable terms to one side and numbers to the other, then divide.
Always substitute the answer back to check.
mistakes: Changing the sign of only one side when moving a term across.

title: Algebraic identities
subject: Mathematics
summary: An identity is true for every value of its variables, and the standard identities let you expand and factorise quickly.
points: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
(x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab.
mistakes: Writing (a + b)² as a² + b² and forgetting the 2ab term.

title: Factorisation
subject: Mathematics
summary: Factorisation writes an expression as a product of factors, reversing expansion.
points: Take out the highest common factor first.
Use identities such as a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b).
For x² + (a + b)x + ab, look for two numbers that add to the middle coefficient and multiply to the constant.
mistakes: Writing x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 5)(x + 1); the constants must multiply to 6 as well as add to 5.

title: Lines and angles
subject: Mathematics
summary: Angles are measured in degrees, and the relationships between angles on lines and between parallel lines let you find unknown angles.
points: Angles on a straight line add to 180°; angles around a point add to 360°.
When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, corresponding angles are equal and co-interior angles add to 180°.
Vertically opposite angles are equal.
example: If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal and one angle is 65°, the alternate interior angle is also 65°.
mistakes: Assuming lines are parallel because they look parallel; it must be given.

title: Triangles and their properties
subject: Mathematics
summary: A triangle has three sides and three angles, and its interior angles always add to 180°.
points: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
A triangle is possible only if the sum of any two sides is greater than the third.
Triangles are classified by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles (acute, right, obtuse).
example: Angles 50° and 60° leave 70° for the third angle, because 180 − 50 − 60 = 70.
mistakes: Using the exterior angle as if it were inside the triangle.

title: Quadrilaterals and polygons
subject: Mathematics
summary: A quadrilateral has four sides, and its interior angles add to 360°; special quadrilaterals have their own properties.
points: A parallelogram has opposite sides parallel and equal, and opposite angles equal.
A rectangle has four right angles; a rhombus has four equal sides; a square has both.
The angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°.
example: A pentagon has (5 − 2) × 180° = 540° in total.
mistakes: Assuming every parallelogram is a rectangle.

title: Circles
subject: Mathematics
summary: A circle is the set of points at a fixed distance from its centre; the radius, diameter, chord and circumference describe it.
points: Diameter = 2 × radius.
Circumference = 2πr and area = πr².
A tangent touches the circle at one point; a chord joins two points on it.
example: A circle of radius 7 cm has circumference 44 cm and area 154 cm² using π = 22/7.
mistakes: Using the diameter in place of the radius in πr².

title: Mensuration: area and volume
subject: Mathematics
summary: Mensuration finds perimeter, area, surface area and volume of common plane and solid shapes.
points: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height; of a parallelogram = base × height.
Volume of a cuboid = l × b × h; of a cube = side³.
Total surface area of a cuboid = 2(lb + bh + hl).
example: A cuboid 4 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm has volume 24 cm³ and surface area 2(12 + 6 + 8) = 52 cm².
mistakes: Mixing units, such as cm with m, before multiplying.

title: Data handling: mean, median and mode
subject: Mathematics
summary: Mean, median and mode are three ways to describe the centre of a data set.
points: Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values.
Median is the middle value after sorting; with an even count it is the average of the two middle values.
Mode is the value that appears most often.
example: For 3, 7, 7, 9, 12: mean 7.6, median 7, mode 7.
mistakes: Finding the median without sorting the data first.

title: Probability
subject: Mathematics
summary: Probability measures how likely an event is, as a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
points: For equally likely outcomes, P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.
P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
Probabilities of all possible outcomes add to 1.
example: A fair die: P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2, so P(odd) = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2.
mistakes: Writing a probability greater than 1.

title: Measurement and units
subject: Science
summary: Measurement compares a quantity with a standard unit, and SI units keep measurements consistent.
points: SI base units include metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time) and kelvin (temperature).
1 m = 100 cm and 1 kg = 1000 g.
The least count of an instrument is the smallest value it can measure.
example: A pencil measuring 15 cm is 0.15 m.
mistakes: Writing a measurement without its unit.

title: Motion, speed and distance
subject: Physics
summary: An object is in motion if its position changes with time relative to a reference point; speed describes how fast that change happens.
points: Distance is the total path length; displacement is the straight-line change in position with direction.
Speed = distance ÷ time; velocity is speed in a given direction.
Uniform motion means equal distances in equal times.
example: A car covering 150 m in 10 s has an average speed of 15 m/s.
mistakes: Treating distance and displacement as the same thing.

title: Force and friction
subject: Physics
summary: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's speed, direction or shape, and friction is a force opposing motion between surfaces.
points: Forces are measured in newtons and have both size and direction.
Friction depends on the surfaces and how hard they press together; it can be reduced with lubricants or wheels.
Balanced forces do not change motion; unbalanced forces do.
example: A box slides more easily on a smooth floor than on a rough carpet because friction is smaller.
mistakes: Thinking a moving object always has a force pushing it along.

title: Gravitation and pressure
subject: Physics
summary: Gravity pulls objects towards each other, and pressure is force spread over an area.
points: Weight = mass × gravitational acceleration (g ≈ 9.8 m/s² on Earth).
Pressure = force ÷ area, measured in pascals.
A smaller area gives greater pressure for the same force, which is why a sharp knife cuts easily.
example: A 60 kg student weighs about 588 N on Earth.
mistakes: Using mass and weight interchangeably; mass is in kg and weight in newtons.

title: Work and energy
subject: Physics
summary: Work is done when a force moves an object, and energy is the ability to do work.
points: Work = force × distance moved in the direction of the force, measured in joules.
Kinetic energy = ½mv² and gravitational potential energy = mgh.
Energy is conserved: it changes form but is not created or destroyed.
example: Lifting a 2 kg bag by 1.5 m does mgh = 2 × 9.8 × 1.5 ≈ 29.4 J of work.
mistakes: Counting work when the force is perpendicular to the motion, as when carrying a bag horizontally.

title: Heat and temperature
subject: Physics
summary: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; temperature measures how hot or cold something is.
points: Heat flows from a hotter body to a colder one until both reach the same temperature.
Temperature is measured in °C or kelvin; K = °C + 273.
Materials conduct heat at different rates; metals are good conductors.
example: A metal spoon in hot tea warms up because metal conducts heat well.
mistakes: Saying an object contains heat; heat is energy in transfer.

title: Light, reflection and shadows
subject: Physics
summary: Light travels in straight lines; it reflects from surfaces and is blocked by opaque objects to form shadows.
points: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
A plane mirror forms an upright image of the same size, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Transparent, translucent and opaque materials let different amounts of light through.
example: A shadow is formed because light cannot pass through an opaque object.
mistakes: Thinking a shadow has colour and detail; it only shows the outline.

title: Sound
subject: Physics
summary: Sound is a vibration that travels as a wave through a medium and is heard when it reaches the ear.
points: Sound needs a medium, so it cannot travel through a vacuum.
Frequency determines pitch and amplitude determines loudness.
Sound travels faster in solids than in gases.
example: A sound of frequency 500 Hz with wavelength 0.68 m travels at about 340 m/s.
mistakes: Saying sound travels fastest through air; it travels fastest through solids.

title: Electric current and circuits
subject: Physics
summary: An electric current is a flow of charge through a conductor, driven by a potential difference and controlled by resistance.
points: Current is measured in amperes, potential difference in volts and resistance in ohms.
Ohm's law: V = IR at constant temperature.
A series circuit has one path; a parallel circuit has several.

formulas.name: Ohm's law
formulas.symbols: V volts, I amperes, R ohms

example: A 6 V battery across 3 Ω gives a current of 2 A.
mistakes: Adding resistances directly in a parallel circuit instead of using 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.

title: Magnets and magnetism
subject: Physics
summary: Magnets attract magnetic materials and have north and south poles that repel like poles and attract opposite ones.
points: A freely suspended magnet points north–south.
Magnetic field lines run from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet.
Heating or hammering a magnet can weaken it.
example: Two north poles pushed together repel; a north and a south pole attract.
mistakes: Thinking a magnet attracts all metals; it does not attract copper or aluminium.

title: Matter and its states
subject: Chemistry
summary: Matter is anything with mass and volume, and it exists as solid, liquid or gas depending on how its particles are arranged and move.
points: Solids have fixed shape and volume; liquids have fixed volume but take the shape of the container; gases fill the container.
Particles are always in motion, and heating increases that motion.
Changing state is a physical change: melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation and sublimation.
example: Ice melts to water and boils to steam, but the substance remains water.
mistakes: Thinking gas particles disappear or stop moving.

title: Physical and chemical changes
subject: Chemistry
summary: A physical change alters form or state without making a new substance; a chemical change produces a new substance.
points: Chemical changes usually release or absorb energy and are hard to reverse.
Signs include a new colour, gas, heat or a precipitate.
Rusting, burning and cooking are chemical changes; melting and dissolving are usually physical.
example: Burning paper makes ash and gases, a chemical change; tearing paper is only physical.
mistakes: Calling dissolving sugar a chemical change; it can be recovered by evaporation.

title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
subject: Chemistry
summary: An element is one kind of atom, a compound is two or more elements chemically combined, and a mixture contains substances not chemically combined.
points: Compounds have a fixed ratio by mass and properties different from their elements.
Mixtures can be separated by physical methods.
Air is a mixture; water is a compound.
example: Water is H₂O, a compound; salt solution is a mixture that can be separated by evaporation.
mistakes: Calling air a compound; it is a mixture of gases.

title: Separation techniques
subject: Chemistry
summary: Mixtures are separated using differences in properties such as particle size, solubility, boiling point or magnetism.
points: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.
Evaporation recovers a dissolved solid; distillation separates liquids by boiling point.
Handpicking, sieving, threshing and magnetic separation work on visible differences.
example: Sand and water are separated by filtration; salt and water by evaporation.
mistakes: Using filtration to separate salt from water, which needs evaporation.

title: Acids, bases and salts
subject: Chemistry
summary: Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus red; bases taste bitter, feel soapy and turn red litmus blue; they neutralise each other to form salt and water.
points: The pH scale runs from 0 (strongly acidic) through 7 (neutral) to 14 (strongly basic).
Acid + base → salt + water is a neutralisation reaction.
Indicators such as litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein show acidity.
example: Acid indigestion is treated with an antacid base such as magnesium hydroxide.
mistakes: Thinking a pH of 8 is acidic; above 7 is basic.

title: Metals and non-metals
subject: Chemistry
summary: Metals are usually shiny, malleable, ductile and good conductors; non-metals are usually dull, brittle and poor conductors.
points: Metals lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals gain or share electrons.
The reactivity series orders metals by how readily they react.
Displacement occurs when a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its salt.
example: Zinc displaces copper from copper sulphate solution: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
mistakes: Assuming all metals react with water; gold and silver do not.

title: Atoms and molecules
subject: Chemistry
summary: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that keeps its properties; a molecule is two or more atoms bonded together.
points: Protons and neutrons sit in the nucleus; electrons move around it.
Atomic number = number of protons; mass number = protons + neutrons.
A chemical formula shows the atoms in a compound, such as H₂O or CO₂.
example: A water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
mistakes: Confusing atomic number with mass number.

title: Combustion and fuels
subject: Chemistry
summary: Combustion is a chemical reaction with oxygen that releases heat and light, usually producing carbon dioxide and water.
points: A fuel needs oxygen and a temperature above its ignition temperature to burn.
Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water; incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide and soot.
Water and carbon dioxide extinguishers cut off oxygen.
example: Burning methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
mistakes: Treating carbon monoxide as harmless; it binds haemoglobin and is dangerous.

title: The cell
subject: Biology
summary: The cell is the basic unit of life, and its organelles carry out the functions that keep an organism alive.
points: The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves; the nucleus contains genetic material.
Mitochondria release energy; chloroplasts in plant cells carry out photosynthesis.
Plant cells have a cell wall and a large vacuole, which animal cells do not have.
example: A leaf cell has chloroplasts and a cell wall; a cheek cell does not.
mistakes: Thinking animal cells have a cell wall.

title: Tissues
subject: Biology
summary: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together for a particular function.
points: Plant tissues include meristematic tissue for growth, and xylem and phloem for transport.
Animal tissues include epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissue.
Organs are made of several tissues working together.
example: Xylem carries water upward, and phloem carries food made in leaves to the rest of the plant.
mistakes: Mixing up xylem (water) and phloem (food).

title: Photosynthesis
subject: Biology
summary: Photosynthesis is how green plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make glucose and release oxygen, with chlorophyll capturing the light.
points: It happens mainly in the chloroplasts of leaf cells.
Carbon dioxide enters through stomata and water arrives through the roots.
Glucose is used for energy or stored as starch; oxygen is released.
example: A leaf kept in sunlight produces starch, which turns blue-black with iodine.
mistakes: Saying plants get their food from the soil; they make it, and take only water and minerals from soil.

title: Respiration
subject: Biology
summary: Respiration releases energy from glucose inside cells, using oxygen in aerobic respiration and without it in anaerobic respiration.
points: Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.
Anaerobic respiration in muscles produces lactic acid; in yeast it produces alcohol and carbon dioxide.
Respiration is not the same as breathing; breathing brings air in and out.
example: Yeast in dough respires anaerobically and the carbon dioxide makes bread rise.
mistakes: Using respiration and breathing as synonyms.

title: Digestion and absorption
subject: Biology
summary: Digestion breaks food into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood.
points: Digestion begins in the mouth with teeth and saliva.
The stomach adds acid and enzymes; the small intestine completes digestion and absorbs nutrients.
The large intestine absorbs water and forms waste.
example: Starch is broken down by salivary amylase into sugars, starting in the mouth.
mistakes: Thinking most absorption happens in the stomach; it happens mainly in the small intestine.

title: Circulation and excretion
subject: Biology
summary: The heart pumps blood through vessels to carry oxygen and nutrients, and the kidneys filter waste from the blood.
points: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back; capillaries connect them.
The human heart has four chambers and a double circulation.
The kidneys filter blood and produce urine.
example: Blood in the pulmonary artery is deoxygenated, even though it is an artery.
mistakes: Believing all arteries carry oxygenated blood; the pulmonary artery does not.

title: Reproduction in plants and animals
subject: Biology
summary: Reproduction produces new individuals, either asexually from one parent or sexually by the fusion of male and female gametes.
points: Asexual reproduction includes budding, fragmentation and vegetative propagation.
Flowers contain male stamens and female pistils; pollination transfers pollen.
Fertilisation joins gametes to form a zygote.
example: A potato tuber grows into a new plant, which is vegetative propagation.
mistakes: Confusing pollination with fertilisation; pollination comes first.

title: Microorganisms
subject: Biology
summary: Microorganisms are living things too small to see without a microscope, including bacteria, fungi, protozoa and viruses.
points: Some cause disease, while others are useful in food, medicine and decomposition.
Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses.
Handwashing, cooking and refrigeration reduce harmful microbes.
example: Yeast makes bread rise, and Lactobacillus turns milk into curd.
mistakes: Taking antibiotics for a viral cold, which does not help.

title: Ecosystems
subject: Biology
summary: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings.
points: Producers make food, consumers eat it and decomposers break down dead matter.
Energy flows through food chains and is lost as heat at each step.
Biodiversity keeps ecosystems stable and resilient.
example: In a pond ecosystem, algae are producers, small fish eat them and herons eat the fish.
mistakes: Thinking energy cycles; nutrients cycle, but energy flows and is lost.

title: Adaptation
subject: Biology
summary: An adaptation is a feature or behaviour that helps an organism survive in its habitat.
points: Desert plants reduce water loss with thick waxy leaves or spines.
Polar animals have thick fur and a layer of fat.
Adaptations develop over many generations through natural selection.
example: A cactus stores water in its stem and has spines instead of leaves.
mistakes: Saying an animal chooses to adapt; populations change over generations.

title: Indus Valley Civilisation
subject: History
summary: The Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilisation was an urban civilisation of about 2600–1900 BCE in the north-west of the subcontinent, known for planned cities and drainage.
points: Major sites include Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal and Dholavira.
Houses were built with baked bricks, and streets followed a grid plan.
Its script has not been deciphered, so much of its history comes from archaeology.
example: Mohenjo-daro had covered drains and a Great Bath, showing advanced town planning.
mistakes: Claiming the Harappan script has been read; it has not.

title: Vedic period
subject: History
summary: The Vedic period (roughly 1500–500 BCE) is named after the Vedas and saw the growth of early settlements, pastoral life and later kingdoms in northern India.
points: The Rigveda is the oldest Veda and contains hymns.
Early Vedic society was largely pastoral; later Vedic society saw agriculture and towns grow.
The varna system became more rigid in the later Vedic period.
example: The Gayatri Mantra comes from the Rigveda.
mistakes: Treating the Vedic period as a single unchanging society; it changed over centuries.

title: Mauryan Empire
subject: History
summary: The Mauryan Empire (c. 321–185 BCE) was the first large empire in India, founded by Chandragupta Maurya and expanded by Ashoka.
points: Chanakya (Kautilya) wrote the Arthashastra on statecraft and economy.
Ashoka's edicts spread messages of dhamma after the Kalinga war.
The empire had a strong administration with provinces and officials.
example: Ashoka's pillars and rock edicts are important sources for Mauryan history.
mistakes: Thinking Ashoka founded the empire; Chandragupta did.

title: Gupta Empire
subject: History
summary: The Gupta Empire (c. 320–550 CE) is remembered for political unity, literature, science and art, and is often called a golden age of classical India.
points: Chandragupta I, Samudragupta and Chandragupta II were major rulers.
Aryabhata worked on astronomy and mathematics, including the place-value system.
Temples, sculpture and Sanskrit literature flourished.
example: Kalidasa wrote plays and poetry such as Abhijnanashakuntalam during this period.
mistakes: Assuming the 'golden age' was equally golden for everyone; it refers mainly to elite culture.

title: Delhi Sultanate
subject: History
summary: The Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) was a series of five dynasties that ruled much of northern India from Delhi.
points: The five dynasties were the Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties.
Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughlaq carried out major administrative and military changes.
The Sultanate saw new architecture, Persian culture and market reforms.
example: Alauddin Khalji fixed prices of goods in the market and reformed the army.
mistakes: Confusing the Delhi Sultanate with the Mughal Empire, which came later.

title: Mughal Empire
subject: History
summary: The Mughal Empire (1526–1857) was founded by Babur after the First Battle of Panipat and became one of the largest empires in Indian history.
points: Akbar expanded the empire and promoted sulh-i kul, a policy of tolerance.
Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort.
Aurangzeb's reign and later conflicts weakened the empire.
example: The First Battle of Panipat in 1526 established Mughal rule in northern India.
mistakes: Thinking the Taj Mahal was built by Akbar; Shah Jahan built it.

title: Indian freedom movement
subject: History
summary: The Indian freedom movement grew from early reform and revolt into a mass struggle for independence, led by the Indian National Congress and many others.
points: The Revolt of 1857 was a major uprising against Company rule.
Gandhi's Non-Cooperation (1920), Civil Disobedience (1930) and Quit India (1942) movements mobilised millions.
India became independent on 15 August 1947, with Partition creating Pakistan.
example: The Dandi March of 1930 began the Civil Disobedience Movement against the salt tax.
mistakes: Treating the movement as the work of a single leader; it involved many groups and people.

title: Earth and its structure
subject: Geography
summary: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and has three main layers: the crust, mantle and core.
points: The crust is the thin outer layer; the mantle lies beneath it; the core is at the centre.
Earth's rotation causes day and night, and its revolution around the Sun causes seasons.
About 71% of Earth's surface is water.
example: The Earth completes one rotation in about 24 hours and one revolution in about 365¼ days.
mistakes: Saying seasons are caused by distance from the Sun; they are caused by Earth's tilted axis.

title: Latitudes and longitudes
subject: Geography
summary: Latitudes are imaginary horizontal lines measured north and south of the equator, and longitudes are vertical lines measured east and west of the prime meridian.
points: The equator is 0° latitude; the Tropic of Cancer is 23.5° N.
Longitudes are used for time zones; 15° of longitude corresponds to one hour.
The prime meridian passes through Greenwich.
example: India's standard time is based on 82.5° E, which is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.
mistakes: Confusing latitude lines (horizontal) with longitude lines (vertical).

title: Landforms
subject: Geography
summary: Landforms are natural shapes of the land, such as mountains, plateaus, plains, valleys and deserts, shaped by internal and external forces.
points: Mountains are high land with steep slopes; plateaus are elevated flat areas; plains are low and flat.
Rivers, glaciers, wind and waves erode and deposit material.
Fold mountains form where tectonic plates collide.
example: The Himalayas are fold mountains formed by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates.
mistakes: Thinking landforms are permanent; they change over long periods.

title: Rivers and drainage
subject: Geography
summary: A river is a natural flow of water from higher to lower ground, and a drainage basin is the area it collects water from.
points: The three stages of a river are upper, middle and lower course.
Himalayan rivers are perennial; peninsular rivers are seasonal.
Rivers build deltas, floodplains and meanders.
example: The Ganga and Brahmaputra form the Sundarbans delta, the largest delta in the world.
mistakes: Calling every river mouth a delta; some form estuaries instead.

title: Climate and the monsoon
subject: Geography
summary: Climate is the long-term pattern of weather, and the Indian monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds that brings most of India's rainfall.
points: The monsoon arrives from the south-west in June and retreats from September.
Differences in heating of land and sea, and the Himalayas, shape the monsoon.
India has tropical, arid, coastal and mountain climate regions.
example: Mawsynram in Meghalaya receives some of the highest rainfall in the world because of the monsoon and the hills.
mistakes: Treating weather and climate as identical; one is day to day, the other long term.

title: Natural vegetation and wildlife
subject: Geography
summary: Natural vegetation is the plant cover that grows without human planting, and it depends on climate and soil.
points: Tropical rainforests grow in hot, wet regions; deciduous forests shed leaves in dry seasons.
Grasslands, thorn forests, mangroves and alpine vegetation each suit different conditions.
Wildlife is adapted to each habitat and protected in national parks and sanctuaries.
example: Sundari trees grow in the Sundarbans mangroves, which are adapted to salty water.
mistakes: Thinking forests are the same everywhere; they vary with rainfall and temperature.

title: Resources and their types
subject: Geography
summary: Resources are things from the environment that people use, and they can be natural or human-made, renewable or non-renewable.
points: Renewable resources such as sunlight and wind are naturally replenished.
Non-renewable resources such as coal and petroleum are limited.
Sustainable use keeps resources available for future generations.
example: Solar energy is renewable; coal is non-renewable.
mistakes: Calling groundwater unlimited; it can be over-extracted.

title: Agriculture
subject: Geography
summary: Agriculture is the cultivation of crops and rearing of animals, and its types depend on land, water, climate and technology.
points: Subsistence farming feeds the farmer's family; commercial farming sells produce.
Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon and rabi crops in winter.
Irrigation, fertilisers and mechanisation raise yields but can harm the environment.
example: Rice is a kharif crop, while wheat is mainly a rabi crop in India.
mistakes: Mixing up kharif (monsoon) and rabi (winter) seasons.

title: Population
subject: Geography
summary: Population geography studies how many people live where, how they are distributed and how numbers change.
points: Population density = population ÷ area.
Birth rate, death rate and migration change population.
A population pyramid shows the age and sex structure.
example: A region with 500,000 people in 1,000 km² has a density of 500 people per km².
mistakes: Confusing population growth with population density.

title: Democracy
subject: Civics
summary: Democracy is a system where people choose their rulers and hold them accountable through free and fair elections.
points: Key features include universal adult franchise, rule of law and respect for rights.
Elections must be free, fair and held regularly.
Democracy also needs an informed public and protection of minorities.
example: In India, every citizen aged 18 or above can vote regardless of caste, religion or gender.
mistakes: Equating democracy with majority rule alone; rights and accountability also matter.

title: The Indian Constitution
subject: Civics
summary: The Constitution is the supreme law of India, adopted on 26 November 1949 and in force from 26 January 1950.
points: It lays down the structure of government, the powers of each branch and citizens' rights.
Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly.
It is a living document that can be amended.
example: The Preamble declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic.
mistakes: Saying the Constitution came into force in 1949; it was adopted then and enforced in 1950.

title: Fundamental rights and duties
subject: Civics
summary: Fundamental rights protect citizens against the state, and fundamental duties are responsibilities the Constitution expects of citizens.
points: Rights include equality, freedom, protection from exploitation, religion, culture and education, and constitutional remedies.
Article 32 allows a person to approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of rights.
Fundamental duties were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.
example: The right to education (Article 21A) makes free education a right for children aged 6–14.
mistakes: Thinking fundamental rights are absolute; reasonable restrictions apply.

title: Local government and Panchayati Raj
subject: Civics
summary: Local government handles local matters through panchayats in villages and municipal bodies in towns.
points: The 73rd Amendment (1992) gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj.
A gram panchayat is elected by the village and works with the gram sabha.
One-third of seats are reserved for women in local bodies.
example: A gram panchayat can maintain village roads, water supply and street lighting.
mistakes: Thinking panchayats are appointed; they are elected.

title: Parliament and the judiciary
subject: Civics
summary: Parliament makes laws for the country, and the judiciary interprets the Constitution and settles disputes.
points: Parliament has the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
The Supreme Court is the highest court, and judicial review lets it strike down unconstitutional laws.
The judiciary is independent of the legislature and executive.
example: A bill becomes an Act after both Houses pass it and the President assents.
mistakes: Saying the President makes laws alone; Parliament legislates.

title: Diversity and equality
subject: Civics
summary: India is diverse in language, religion, culture and region, and equality means every person has the same rights and dignity.
points: Diversity is protected by the right to freedom of religion and culture.
The Constitution forbids discrimination on grounds such as religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
Prejudice and stereotypes create inequality and must be challenged.
example: Article 15 prohibits discrimination in public places and employment.
mistakes: Thinking equality means treating everyone identically regardless of need; it can require support for disadvantaged groups.

title: Computer fundamentals
subject: Computer Science
summary: A computer takes input, processes it with a CPU, stores results and gives output, following instructions called programs.
points: Hardware is the physical parts; software is the set of instructions.
Main memory (RAM) is temporary; storage such as a hard disk keeps data permanently.
Input devices include keyboards and cameras; output devices include screens and printers.
example: Typing a letter uses the keyboard (input), RAM and CPU (processing), and the screen (output).
mistakes: Confusing memory with storage; RAM loses its contents when power is off.

title: Internet basics and online safety
subject: Computer Science
summary: The internet is a network of networks that lets computers share information, and staying safe online means protecting accounts, data and privacy.
points: The web is one service on the internet; browsers request pages using HTTP or HTTPS.
Use strong, different passwords and enable two-factor authentication.
Phishing messages pretend to be trusted senders to steal information.
example: A bank will not ask for your password by email; such a message is likely phishing.
mistakes: Reusing one password everywhere, so one leak exposes every account.

title: Algorithms and flowcharts
subject: Computer Science
summary: An algorithm is a finite sequence of clear steps that solves a problem, and a flowchart draws those steps with standard symbols.
points: An algorithm must be finite, unambiguous and produce a result.
Flowchart symbols: oval for start/end, parallelogram for input/output, rectangle for process, diamond for decision.
Pseudocode writes an algorithm in plain structured language.
example: To find the larger of two numbers: read A and B; if A > B, print A; otherwise print B.
mistakes: Writing steps that never end, so the algorithm is not finite.

title: Programming basics
subject: Computer Science
summary: Programming means writing precise instructions for a computer using variables, conditions, loops and functions.
points: A variable stores a value under a name; data types decide what kind of value it holds.
Conditionals choose between paths, and loops repeat work.
A function groups reusable steps and can take inputs and return a result.
example:
```python
total = 0
for n in range(1, 6):
    total += n
print(total)  # 15
```
mistakes: Using a variable before giving it a value.
Writing a loop that never changes its condition, so it never ends.
